So it is that the forest edge belongs to a tidy hunter with many voices.

facts.text: The ring-necked duck is a diving duck from North America commonly found in freshwater ponds and lakes.
Ducklings are dependent on animal matter such as insects, earthworms, leeches, midges and snails.
The main breeding area is Northwest boreal forest territories.
As they mature they tend change their diet to submerged plants such as pondweed and coontail, and emergents such as annual wild rice and snails.
The nest is bowl-shaped, built on water in dense emergent vegetation with sedges and woody plants.
The female lays one egg per day until 8 to 10 eggs are laid.
They are incubated 25–29 days and the female may remain with the young until they are able to fly.
The scientific name is derived from Greek aithuia, an unidentified seabird mentioned by authors including Hesychius and Aristotle, and Latin collaris, "of the neck" from collum, "neck".
Its wingspan is about 71 cm.
It weighs about 705 g.
It feeds mostly on water plants.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a platform or a cup.
It lays 6 to 14 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where the ring-necked duck keeps: on the freshwater ponds and lakes of North America, where it dives.
In the northwest boreal forests it builds a bowl-shaped nest on the water itself, hidden in dense sedges and woody plants.
The mother lays an egg a day and may stay with her young until they can fly.
So it is that ducklings feast on insects, leeches and snails, then grow to favor pondweed, coontail and wild rice.

tagline.text: From insects to pondweed: the diver of freshwater ponds.

facts.text: The oak titmouse is a passerine bird in the tit family Paridae.
Specifically, following with the low predation, it has contributed to oak titmouse’s high nest failure.
The oak titmouse builds its nest in a woodpecker hole, a natural cavity, or a nest box, using grass, moss, mud, hair, feathers, and fur.
The song of the oak titmouse is a series of repeated phrases of two or three notes with the last note of lower pitch; usually, three to seven phrases are grouped together.
When roosting in foliage, the titmouse chooses a twig surrounded by dense foliage or an accumulation of dead pine needles, simulating a roost in a cavity.
Their role in nesting differs slightly:, the female builds the nest over 4 to 10 days, and males often accompany her, and bring her food during the nesting process.
And the call is a scratchy tsicka-dee-dee.
The oak titmouse is a small, brown-tinged gray bird with a small tuft or crest.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 21 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 16 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays 6 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The small gray oak titmouse, tufted crown and all, nests in a woodpecker hole, a natural cavity, or a nest box.
The female builds it of grass, moss, mud, hair, feathers and fur, as the male brings her food.
Even away from the nest, it roosts on a twig wrapped in thick leaves, or in dead pine needles, as if inside a cavity.
So the tale goes: it has never forgotten the shape of a hole.

tagline.text: It carries a hollow with it, even among the leaves.

facts.text: The cedar waxwing is a member of the family Bombycillidae or waxwing family of passerine birds.
Its diet includes cedar cones, fruit, holly berries, and insects.
Cedar waxwings are sociable, seen in flocks year round.
During courtship, the male and female sit together and pass small objects back and forth, such as flower petals or an insect.
The two common calls of these birds include very high-pitched whistles and buzzy trills about a half-second long, often represented as see or sree.

Vieillot thought that motacilla, Latin for wagtails, was derived from mota for "move" and cilla, which he thought meant "tail"; however, Motacilla actually combines motacis, a mover, with the diminutive suffix -illa.
They are frequently seen in fruiting trees.
Populations are increasing in their range partly because fields are being allowed to grow into forests and shrublands, and fruiting trees such as mountain ash are being planted as landscaping.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 29 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 32 g.
It feeds mostly on fruit.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the cedar waxwing travels in flocks the whole year round, and the tale points to the fruiting trees.
There the birds gather over cedar cones, holly berries and fruit, filling the branches with high whistles and buzzy trills, see and sree.
A feast so plentiful must be shared, the story goes, and so it is that a courting pair sits side by side, passing a flower petal or an insect back and forth.

tagline.text: The flock that feasts together, and courts with gifts.

facts.text: The Canada goose is a large species of goose with a black head and neck, white cheeks, white under its chin, and a brown body.
The last is a result of humans not following artificial feeding policies toward wild animals.
The calls overhead from large groups of Canada geese flying in a V-shaped formation signal the transitions into spring and autumn.
During the second year of their lives, Canada geese find a mate.
An extended hunting season, deploying noise makers, and hazing by dogs have been used in an attempt to disrupt suspect flocks.
The geese are considered protected, though a hunting season is allowed in September.
The British longevity record is held by a specimen tagged as a nestling, which was observed alive at the University of York at the age of 31.
The honk refers to the call of the male Canada goose, whilst the hrink call refers to the female goose.
Its wingspan is about 160 cm.
It weighs about 2.8 kg.
It feeds mostly on plants.
It lives mostly in grassland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the sky grows loud.
Look up and see the Canada goose, black of head and neck, white of cheek, brown of body, flying with its flock in a great V.
Their calls overhead tell the land that spring or autumn is coming.
Listen closely, and the song has two voices: the male gives the honk, the female the hrink.
So the story goes, the pair learn this duet in their second year, when the geese find a mate.

tagline.text: Honk and hrink overhead: the seasons are turning.

facts.text: The yellow-chevroned parakeet is native to tropical South America south of the Amazon River basin from central Brazil to southern Bolivia, Paraguay, and northern Argentina.
The bird feeds mostly on seeds and fruit in its native habitat, and feral populations have adapted to eat blossoms and nectar.
Yellow-chevroned parakeets usually find holes in trees for nesting.
During dry periods, which often leads to fruit scarcity, the bird adapts by eating more seeds, particularly from the plant Erythrina dominguezii.
The female lays four to five eggs.
Wild birds primarily use disturbed forests and forest clearings around settlements.
A small population in San Francisco, California that mostly centered around Mission Dolores Park disappeared in the early 2000s.
They rarely use deep tropical forests.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 34 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 62 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 5 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the yellow-chevroned parakeet keeps to forest clearings and broken woods near settlements, and seldom flies into the deep tropical forest.
It feeds mostly on seeds and fruit, but when dry times leave the fruit scarce, it eats more seeds, most of all from Erythrina dominguezii.
The tale answers that a bird of the edges always knows where another meal waits.
And for its nest, it seeks out a hole in a tree and settles there.

tagline.text: The edge-dweller who turns to seeds when the fruit runs short.

facts.text: The great horned owl, also known as the tiger owl or the hoot owl, is a large owl native to the Americas.
Its diet consists primarily of rabbits and hares, rats and mice, and voles; it remains one of the few regular predators of skunk.
In most aspects of their behavior, great horned owls are typical of owls and most birds of prey.
In most of North America, courtship is from October to December and mates are chosen by December to January.
The great horned owl's song is normally a low-pitched but loud ho-ho-hoo hoo hoo and can last for four or five syllables.
Hunting and trapping of great horned owls may continue on a small scale but is now illegal in most countries.

In prairies, grasslands and deserts, they can successfully live year-round as long as there are rocky canyons, steep gullies and/or wooded coulees with shade-giving trees to provide shelter and nesting sites.
Occasionally, these owls may prey on threatened species.
Its wingspan is about 134 cm.
It weighs about 1.4 kg.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
It lays 1 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Across the Americas, in rocky canyons, steep gullies and shady coulees, the hoot owl keeps its shelter and nest the whole year round.
Its song is low but loud: ho-ho-hoo, hoo, hoo.
It hunts rabbits and hares, rats, mice and voles.
Ask why the tiger owl is one of the few hunters that will take a skunk, and the tale answers: a bird named for the tiger turns from no meal.

tagline.text: Low but loud, the tiger owl calls from the canyons.

facts.text: The bufflehead is a small sea duck of the genus Bucephala, the goldeneyes.
Buffleheads have evolved their small size to fit the nesting cavity of their "metabiotic" host, a woodpecker, the northern flicker.
Nest competitors include mountain bluebird, tree swallow, and European starling.
Buffleheads are hunted and are considered a gamebird.
Due to their small size, they are highly active, undertaking dives almost continuously while sustained by their high metabolism.
Females may be killed on the nest by mammals, such as foxes, weasels or mink, and by goldeneyes over nest competition.
The bufflehead, also known as the spirit duck, was added to the coat of arms of the town of Sidney, British Columbia, in 1995.
They are migratory and most of them winter in protected coastal waters, or open inland waters, on the east and west coasts of North America and the southern United States.
Its wingspan is about 59 cm.
It weighs about 398 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 5 to 14 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the bufflehead, the spirit duck, is so small, and the tale answers: it shaped itself to fit a door.
Its nest is the hollow of a woodpecker, the northern flicker, and the little sea duck fits it well.
Being small, it is never still: it dives and dives again, almost without rest, kept going by a high metabolism.
Most winter in sheltered coastal and open inland waters of North America.

tagline.text: Sized for a woodpecker's door, it dives and dives again.

facts.text: The red-tailed hawk is a bird of prey and one of the most common hawks in North America.
It breeds from central Alaska, the Yukon, and the Northwest Territories east to southern Quebec and the Maritime Provinces of Canada, and south to Florida, the West Indies, and Central America.
In general, the red-tailed hawk only takes a new mate when its original mate dies.
The red-tailed hawk frequently vocalizes while hunting or soaring, but vocalizes loudest in annoyance or anger, in response to a predator or a rival hawk's intrusion into its territory.
Shorter primaries result in wingtips that don't reach the tail in perched birds.
The species feeds on a wide range of small animals, such as rodents, birds, and reptiles.
Its preferred habitat is mixed forest and field, with high bluffs or trees that may be used as perch sites.
The same nesting territory may be defended by the pair for years.
Its wingspan is about 122 cm.
It weighs about 1.1 kg.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Where mixed forest meets open field, the red-tailed hawk keeps watch from high bluffs and tall trees.
It hunts rodents, birds and reptiles.
It calls as it soars and as it hunts, but ask why its cry rings loudest, and the tale answers: a rival hawk or a predator has crossed its ground.
That ground belongs to a pair, who may defend it for years.
So it is that a red-tail weds again only when its mate dies.

tagline.text: It calls loudest when rivals cross its ground.

facts.text: The red-shouldered hawk is a medium-sized buteo.
Red-shouldered hawks search for prey while perched on a treetop or soaring over woodlands.
They have been known to nest near residential areas and open water but this is much less common.
Red-shouldered hawks typically migrate alone, although they sometimes form small flocks of three or more birds.
Local forest regrowth and the ban of hunting has allowed red-shouldered hawk populations to become more stable again and the species is not currently considered conservation dependent.
Red "shoulders" are visible when the birds are perched.
When they sight prey, they kill it by dropping directly onto it from the air.
Red-shouldered hawks select sites with greater tree species richness for nesting.
Its wingspan is about 101 cm.
It weighs about 604 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in woodland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It lays 2 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the red-shouldered hawk keeps to the treetops, and the woods will answer with a story.
From a high treetop perch, or soaring over the woodlands, this medium-sized hawk searches for prey.
When it sights prey, it drops straight down onto it from the air, and the hunt is done.
Its red shoulders show when it sits perched, the badge of a patient watcher.
For its nest, it chooses woods rich in many kinds of trees.

tagline.text: Watcher of the treetops, dropping straight down from the sky.

facts.text: The green heron is a small heron of North and Central America.
The habitat and foraging area of the green heron includes riparian zones, wetlands, ponds, and lakes, as well as human-made canals and ditches.
The green heron's call is a loud and sudden kyow; it also makes a series of more subdued kuk calls.
Green herons do not exhibit a particular preference for diurnal or nocturnal foraging, often engaging in both.
During courtship, the male gives a raah-rahh call with wide-open bill, makes noisy wingbeats and whoom-whoom-whoom calls in flight, and sometimes calls roo-roo to the female before landing again.
Individuals from the Pacific coast of North America may similarly stray as far as Hawaii.
The color variation between populations is less pronounced than between birds of the same population.
Butorides is from Middle English butor "bittern" and Ancient Greek -oides, "resembling", and virescens is Latin for "greenish".
Its wingspan is about 68 cm.
It weighs about 202 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: Along ponds and lakes, and even in the ditches people dig, the small green heron keeps watch over the water.
It fishes by sun and by dark alike, choosing neither one over the other.
Its voice is a loud and sudden kyow, with quieter kuk calls between.
But in courting time, so the story goes, the male sings his whole heart: raah-rahh with bill flung wide, whoom-whoom-whoom on noisy wings, and roo-roo to his mate before he lands.

tagline.text: Kyow! The little green fisher of day and dark.

facts.text: The Muscovy duck is a species of duck native to the Americas, from the Lower Rio Grande Valley of Texas and Mexico south to Argentina and Uruguay.
The diet consists of plant material obtained by grazing or dabbling in shallow water, and small fish, amphibians, reptiles, crustaceans, spiders, insects, millipedes, and worms.
They will mate on land or in water.
The drake has a low breathy call, and the hen a quiet trilling coo.
It is an aggressive duck; males often fight over food, territory or mates.
The female lays a clutch of 8–15 white eggs, usually in a tree hole or hollow, which are incubated for 30–31 days.
It is not quite clear how the term came about; it very likely originated between 1550 and 1600, but did not become widespread until somewhat later.
The plumage is predominantly black, with large white patches on the wing; the back and wing feathers being iridescent and glossy in males, while the females are more drab.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 126 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 2.4 kg.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It stays in its range all year.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cavity.
It lays 8 to 15 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the Muscovy duck speaks so softly, and the tale points to the wetlands of the Americas.
There the drake gives only a low, breathy call, and the hen a quiet, trilling coo.
The drakes, so the story goes, spent their loud voices long ago on fighting, for they still quarrel over food and mates.
The hen keeps to a tree hole, warming up to fifteen white eggs.

tagline.text: Glossy drake, quiet hen, and a nest in a tree hole.

facts.text: The sanderling is a small wading bird.
It is highly gregarious in winter, sometimes forming large flocks on coastal mudflats or sandy beaches.
Sanderlings feed on invertebrate prey buried in the sand in the upper intertidal zone.
At breeding time sanderlings are territorial, with the male aggressively defending its territory.
During the winter and its migration, it is most commonly found on coastal sandy beaches, but also occurs on tidal sand flats, mud flats and the shores of lakes and rivers.
It eats small crabs and other small invertebrates.
In North America, this diet largely consists of the isopods Excirolana linguifrons, Excirolana kincaidii, and the mole crab, Emerita analoga.
In spring, birds migrating north from South America consume large numbers of horseshoe crab eggs in the Delaware Bay area.
Its wingspan is about 35 cm.
It weighs about 52 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the sanderling, a small wader, keeps to sandy beaches in winter.
The tale answers that the sand hides its food: small crabs and tiny creatures buried high on the shore.
So they gather there in great flocks, glad of company.
Flying north in spring, they feast on horseshoe crab eggs at Delaware Bay.
But at breeding time each male fiercely guards his own ground.

tagline.text: The small wader that finds its feast beneath the sand.

facts.text: The western sandpiper is a small migratory shorebird.
Foraging occurs on tundra and wet meadows during the breeding season.
They nest on the ground usually under some vegetation.
They had been thought to mainly eat insects, spiders, small crustaceans, mollusks, polychaete worms, and seeds, but are now known to heavily graze on biofilm from the surface of intertidal mudflats.
The male makes several scrapes; the female selects one and lays four eggs.
They migrate to both coasts of North America and South America, as well as the Caribbean.
It is a very rare vagrant to western Europe.
Adults have dark legs and a short, thin, dark bill, thinner at the tip.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 31 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 28 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the western sandpiper, a small shorebird, wears so short and thin a bill, finer at the tip.
For years, people thought it ate insects, spiders, worms and seeds.
But the mudflats know better: it grazes biofilm from the mud's surface, and the tale answers that its fine bill was made for that feast.
When it nests, the male scrapes several hollows on the ground, and the female chooses one for her four eggs.

tagline.text: The mudflat grazer with the fine-tipped bill.

facts.text: The least sandpiper is the smallest shorebird.
They mainly eat small crustaceans, insects, and snails.
They nest on the ground near water.
While migrating through the Delaware Bay, least sandpipers eat worms, detritus, and the eggs of horseshoe crabs.
The female lays four eggs in a shallow scrape lined with grass and moss.
The young birds feed themselves and are able to fly within two weeks of birth.
They migrate in flocks to the southern United States, Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean, and northern South America.
Breeding adults are brown with dark brown streaks on top and white underneath.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 30 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 23 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: The least sandpiper, smallest of all the shorebirds, makes its nest on the ground near water.
The nest is a shallow scrape lined with grass and moss, where the female lays her eggs.
Ask why the chicks grow up so fast, and the tale answers that so small a bird has no time to waste.
Within two weeks of birth the young feed themselves and fly.
Then they travel in flocks to Mexico, the Caribbean and northern South America.

tagline.text: Smallest of shorebirds, quick to feed and fly on its own.

facts.text: The California quail, also known as the California valley quail or Valley quail, is a small ground-dwelling bird in the New World quail family, inhabiting western North America.
The California quail is a highly sociable bird that often gathers in small flocks known as "coveys".
The nest is a shallow scrape lined with vegetation on the ground beneath a shrub or other cover.
They can sometimes be seen feeding at the sides of roads.
Once hatched, the young associate with both adults.
Adult males are gray and brown colored, with a black face outlined by white stripes.
It was established as the state bird in 1931.
Females are a plainer brown color and do not have the facial stripes.
It weighs about 166 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 26 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the California quail walks the ground of western North America in little bands called coveys.
The tale answers that it is a bird made for company, too sociable to wander alone.
Its nest is only a shallow scrape, lined with plants and tucked beneath a shrub.
When the chicks hatch, they keep close to both mother and father.
The father's black face, outlined in white stripes, is a lamp for them, they say.

tagline.text: Ground-walker of the west, gathered in coveys.

facts.text: Anna's hummingbird is a North American species of hummingbird named after Anna Masséna, Duchess of Rivoli.

Year-round residence of Anna's hummingbirds in the Pacific Northwest is an example of ecological release dependent on acclimation to colder winter temperatures, introduced plants, and human provision of nectar feeders during winter.
Anna's hummingbirds capture flying insects or eat insects trapped in spider webs, sometimes even the spiders themselves.
The female raises the young without the assistance of the male.
Unlike most northern temperate hummingbirds, the male Anna's hummingbird sings during courtship.
Male birds with elevated levels of protein in their diet have more colorful crowns and higher iridescence in their head feathers compared with male birds with low protein intake.
The female bird builds a nest in a shrub or tree, in vines, or attached to wires or other artificial substrates.
The song is thin and squeaky, interspersed with buzzes and chirps, and is drawn to over 10 seconds in duration.
Its wingspan is about 12 cm.
It weighs about 4.2 g.
It feeds mostly on nectar.
It lives mostly in woodland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why Anna's hummingbird robs the spider.
It snatches flying insects, or plucks them from spider webs, and sometimes eats the spider too.
So it is that the male, well fed on such fare, wears a brighter crown, or so the story goes.
Unlike most hummingbirds of the north, he sings to court, a thin, squeaky song of buzzes and chirps.
The female alone builds the nest and raises the young.

tagline.text: The singing hummingbird that robs the spider's web.

facts.text: The cactus wren is a species of wren that is endemic to the deserts of the southwestern United States and northern and central Mexico.
Their song is a loud raspy chirrup; akin in the description of some ornithologists to the sound of a car engine that will not start.
Cactus wrens generally feed and live in pairs, or in family groups from late spring through winter.
Cactus wrens form permanent pair bonds, and the pairs defend a territory where they live year-round.
The main call of the cactus wren is a harsh and raspy series of jar-jar-jar, or char, notes, which increase in volume and pitch as the song goes on.
The cactus wren is a bird of arid and semi-desert regions, and generally requires spiny cacti to nest in.
Nests built in cactus provide a degree of protection to young; yet even in a cactus, young wrens are vulnerable to predation by coachwhip snakes.
Worn feathers are replaced by molting, which happens in adults from July through October, usually in the bird's own territory.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 25 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 39 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a domed nest.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In the deserts of the southwestern United States and Mexico, the cactus wren keeps a mate for life and a territory all year.
It builds among the spines of cactus, and the spines give its young some shelter, though even there the coachwhip snake may hunt them.
Ask why its song is harsh, and the tale answers: it is a warning, a raspy jar-jar-jar that rises louder and higher, like an engine that will not start.

tagline.text: It sings like an engine that will not start.

facts.text: Wilson's warbler is a small New World warbler.
Wilson's warbler is an insectivore, feeding primarily on insects gleaned from leaves and twigs, or caught by flycatching.
Nesting generally begins in early March in west coast populations, and extends into August in the northern range.
Its song is a chattering series of loud descending notes.
Wilson's warbler is an active forager, moving rapidly through shrubs, on the ground, and sometimes in taller trees during the winter.
The female does the majority of the nest building.
The call is a flat "chuff".
The breeding habitat is fairly open woodland with undergrowth or shrubs and thickets in moist areas with streams, ponds, bogs, and wet clearings.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 18 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 7 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup or a crevice.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Down where streams run through thickets and wet clearings, the small Wilson's warbler keeps its busy court.
It never seems to rest, darting through shrubs and over the ground, picking insects from leaves and twigs or snatching them from the air.
Ask why its song tumbles downward in loud, chattering notes, and the tale answers that a bird this hurried has no time to sing uphill.
Its other voice is one flat word: chuff.

tagline.text: Never still, it sings its songs downhill.

facts.text: The turkey vulture is the most widespread of the New World vultures.
The turkey vulture is a scavenger and feeds almost exclusively on carrion.
The turkey vulture is gregarious and roosts in large community groups, breaking away to forage independently during the day.
Courtship rituals of the turkey vulture involve several individuals gathering in a circle, where they perform hopping movements around the perimeter of the circle with wings partially spread.
The turkey vulture does not kill live animals but will mix with flocks of black vultures and will scavenge what they leave behind.

It is a medium-sized blackbird whose call is a sharp check, easy to tell apart.

The tale answers that it guards an old bond: the same pair tends to reunite each mating season, and both parents share the feeding.
In colder months, they flock together to forage.

tagline.text: The sharp-voiced guardian that dives at hawks.

facts.text: The peregrine falcon, also referred to simply as the peregrine, is a bird of prey in the family Falconidae known for its speed.
In mild-winter regions, it is usually a permanent resident, and some individuals, especially adult males, will remain on the breeding territory.
A pair mates for life and returns to the same nesting spot annually.
It is likely the name was used as juvenile birds were taken while journeying to their breeding location, as falcon nests are often difficult to get at.
Peregrines now breed in many mountainous and coastal areas, especially in the west and north, and nest in some urban areas, capitalising on the urban feral pigeon populations for food.
The upper beak is notched near the tip, an adaptation which enables falcons to kill prey by severing the spinal column at the neck.
Although its diet consists almost exclusively of medium-sized birds, the peregrine will sometimes hunt small mammals, small reptiles, or even insects.
The peregrine falcon's diet varies greatly and is adapted to available prey in different regions.
Its wingspan is about 94 cm.
It weighs about 760 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in grassland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the peregrine keeps to mountains, to coasts, and now to busy cities.
The tale answers that it follows the city pigeons, for it feeds on them there.
Known for its speed, this bird of prey hunts mostly medium-sized birds.
Its upper beak has a notch near the tip, so it can kill by cutting the spine at the neck.
So it is that a pair mates for life and returns each year to the same nesting spot.

tagline.text: The swift one who keeps one mate and one nest.

facts.text: The American kestrel is the smallest and most common falcon in the Americas.
The American kestrel usually hunts in an energy-conserving fashion by perching and scanning the ground for prey to ambush, though it also hunts from the air.
A kestrel's habitat must include perches, open space for hunting, and cavities for nesting.
In migratory populations, the males arrive at the breeding ground before females, then the female selects a mate.
The "whine" call is primarily associated with feeding but is also uttered during copulation.
Several other colloquial names for the kestrel are also in use, including grasshopper hawk, due to its diet, and killy hawk, due to its distinct call.
The Peregrine Fund, a leading non-profit organization advancing research and conservation of birds of prey worldwide, launched the American Kestrel Partnership in 2012.
Their less muscular body type is adapted to energy-conserving ambush hunting, rather than spending large amounts of energy-consuming time on the wing and getting into long tail-chases of bird prey.
Its wingspan is about 55 cm.
It weighs about 115 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in grassland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the smallest falcon of the Americas sits so still upon its perch.
It keeps to open ground, with perches to watch from and hollows to nest in.
There it waits, scanning the ground below, then strikes from ambush.
The tale answers that its lean body was never built for long chases, so it saves its strength for the waiting strike.
Some call it grasshopper hawk for what it eats, and killy hawk for its distinct call.

tagline.text: The little falcon who waits, and watches, and strikes.

facts.text: The American coot, also known as a mud hen or pouldeau, is a bird of the family Rallidae.
The American coot is a highly gregarious species, particularly in the winter, when its flocks can number in the thousands.
Coot mate pairings are monogamous throughout their life, given they have a suitable territory.
The American coot has a variety of repeated calls and sounds.
Coot can be used for cooking; it is somewhat popular in Cajun cuisine, for instance as an ingredient for gumbos cooked at home by duck hunters.

Black American coot chicks have conspicuously orange-tipped ornamental plumes covering the front half of their body that are known as "chick ornaments" that eventually get bleached out after six days.
Coots generally build floating nests and lay 8–12 eggs per clutch.

When swimming on the water surface, American coots exhibit a variety of interesting collective formations, including single-file lines, high density synchronized swimming and rotational dynamics, broad arcing formations, and sequential take-off dynamics.
Its wingspan is about 64 cm.
It weighs about 637 g.
It feeds mostly on water plants.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 6 to 15 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the mud hen gathers in crowds, and the marsh will tell you its tale.
In winter its flocks number in the thousands, swimming in single-file lines, broad arcs and tight bands that turn together.
Its nest floats on the water, and its black chicks wear orange-tipped plumes that bleach away within days.
And the pair that built it, so the story goes, stays together for life, so long as their territory holds.

tagline.text: The mud hen of the marsh, swimming in a crowd.

facts.text: The greater roadrunner is a long-legged bird in the cuckoo family, Cuculidae, from the Aridoamerica region in the Southwestern United States and Mexico.
The greater roadrunner is omnivorous and uses its speed to outrun and catch prey.
Until a mate is found, greater roadrunners typically live a solitary life.
It feeds mainly on small animals, such as insects, spiders, centipedes, scorpions, mice, small birds, lizards and young rattlesnakes, and some plants.
Courtship behaviors between greater roadrunners are a lengthy process including a combination of chasing, tail wagging, play-fighting, and acoustic signals.
Prehistoric remains indicate that until 8,000 years ago, the greater roadrunner was found in sparse forests rather than scrubby deserts; only later did it adapt to arid environments.
Sparse forests can be found in these parts, in an environment similar to the prehistoric North American Southwest.
The vocalizations of the greater roadrunner have seven distinct variants.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 52 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 376 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 2 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: In the dry lands of the Southwestern United States and Mexico, a long-legged cuckoo keeps to the ground, alone until it finds a mate.
It runs down its food, outrunning spiders, lizards and even young rattlesnakes.
Once it walked in thin forests, and only later did it learn the ways of the desert.
So, the tale says, it courts just as it hunts: with chasing, tail wagging and play-fighting.

tagline.text: Born to chase, it hunts and courts on the run.

facts.text: The common yellowthroat is a New World warbler.
Common yellowthroat nests are commonly subject to brood parasitism by the brown-headed cowbird.
Common yellowthroats nest in low vegetation, laying 3–5 eggs in a cup-shaped nest.
The song is a loud twichety twichety twichety twich.
Common yellowthroats here typically migrate to this island during the spring months displaying distinct patterns of movement and stopover ecology.
Its call is a soft jip.
Linnaeus specified the locality as North America but this was restricted to the state of Maryland by the American Ornithologists' Union in 1931.
Despite a decline in numbers, which is due to loss of favored habitat, this species is still very common.
Its wingspan is about 18 cm.
It weighs about 9.5 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Down in the wetlands, the common yellowthroat tucks its cup-shaped nest into low plants.
Ask why this little warbler shouts twichety twichety twichety twich so loudly, when its everyday call is only a soft jip.
The tale answers that it is standing guard, for the brown-headed cowbird often slips its own eggs into the yellowthroat's nest.
So the yellowthroat keeps singing, they say, and though it has lost some of the places it favors, it is still very common.

tagline.text: A loud song rising from low in the wetlands.

facts.text: The black oystercatcher is a conspicuous black bird found on the shoreline of western North America, ranging from the Aleutian Islands of Alaska to the coast of the Baja California peninsula.
It forages in the intertidal zone, feeding on marine invertebrates, particularly molluscs such as mussels, limpets and chitons, but also on crabs, isopods and barnacles.
It forages through the intertidal area, searching for food visually, often so close to the water's edge it has to fly up to avoid crashing surf.
It is the only representative of the oystercatcher family over most of its range, overlapping slightly with the American oystercatcher on the coast of Baja California.
Within its range it is most commonly referred to as the black oystercatcher, although this name is also used locally for the blackish oystercatcher and the African oystercatcher.
It has a bright yellow iris and a red eye-ring.
Its scientific name was derived by John James Audubon from that of his friend John Bachman.
Its plumage varies slightly from north to south, being darker further north.
Its wingspan is about 80 cm.
It weighs about 582 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 4 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: On the shores of western North America, from Alaska to Baja California, walks a conspicuous black bird.
It hunts between the tides, searching by sight for mussels, limpets and chitons.
Ask why it feeds so close to the surf that it must fly up as waves crash.
The tale answers that the sea owes it supper, and it will not step back until paid.
So it stays all year, watching the waves with a yellow eye ringed in red.

tagline.text: It hunts at the water's edge, rising above the crashing surf.

facts.text: The house finch is a North American bird in the finch family.
House finches forage on the ground or in vegetation normally.
Nests are made in cavities, including openings in buildings, hanging plants, and other cup-shaped outdoor decorations.
Analyses of nest records from house finches in California spanning more than a century found that egg‐laying occurred significantly earlier in warmer springs.
The mite Pellonyssus reedi is often found on house finch nestlings, particularly for nests later in the season.
Male coloration varies in intensity with the seasons and is derived from the berries and fruits in its diet.
They primarily eat grains, seeds and berries, being voracious consumers of weed seeds such as nettle and dandelion; included are incidental small insects such as aphids.
Sometimes nests abandoned by other birds are used.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 24 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 21 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where the house finch of North America nests, and look close to home: in openings in buildings, hanging plants and cup-shaped decorations.
Sometimes it moves into a nest another bird left behind.
It forages on the ground and in plants, a hungry eater of seeds, grains and berries.
So it is that the male wears his meals: his color comes from berries and fruits, and it shifts with the seasons.

tagline.text: He wears the berries he eats.

facts.text: The bald eagle is a bird of prey found in North America.
It reaches speeds of 56–70 km/h when gliding and flapping, and about 48 km/h while carrying fish.
Bald eagles have high mate fidelity and generally mate for life.
The Pawnee consider eagles as symbols of fertility because their nests are built high off the ground and because they fiercely protect their young.
In March 2024, bald eagles were found nesting in Toronto for the first time.
Bald eagles, like many birds of prey, were especially affected by DDT due to biomagnification.
The highly developed talon of the hind toe is used to pierce the vital areas of prey while it is held immobile by the front toes.
It is found near large bodies of open water with an abundant food supply and old-growth trees for nesting.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 209 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 4.7 kg.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a half cup.
It lays 1 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where the bald eagle keeps: by large open water rich with food, beside old-growth trees for nesting.
When it hunts, the hind toe's great talon pierces vital places while the front toes hold the prey still.
The Pawnee call it a sign of fertility, for its nest sits high off the ground and it fiercely guards its young.
So the tale says a nest so high needs two keepers, which is why eagles generally mate for life.

tagline.text: Lord of open water, keeper of the high nest.

facts.text: The black-necked stilt, also called the pied stilt, is a locally abundant shorebird of North and South American wetlands and coastlines.
Its mainstay food varies according to availability; inland birds usually feed mainly on aquatic insects and their larvae, while coastal populations mostly eat other aquatic invertebrates.
The nests are typically sited within 1 km of a feeding location, and the pairs defend an extensive perimeter around groups of nests, patrolling in cooperation with their neighbors.
For flocks that summer in the northern Central Valley of California, a migration occurs to the San Joaquin Valley to consolidate with flocks that were already summering there.
Predation by the small Indian mongoose, introduced to hunt rats, is suspected to have contributed to its decline.
For feeding areas they prefer coastal estuaries, salt ponds, lakeshores, alkali flats and even flooded fields.
The nests are frequently established rather close to the water edge, so that their integrity is affected by rising water levels of ponds or tides.
In coastal areas flocks both summer and winter in these estuarine settings.
Its wingspan is about 75 cm.
It weighs about 177 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: The black-necked stilt keeps to the wetlands and coasts of the Americas, feeding at estuaries, salt ponds, lakeshores and even flooded fields.
Inland it hunts water insects and their larvae; on the coast, it takes other water creatures with no backbone.
It sets its nest close to the water's edge, where rising ponds or tides can spoil it.
So, the tale says, the pairs guard a wide ring around their nests, patrolling it together with their neighbors.

tagline.text: Neighbors on patrol at the water's edge.

facts.text: The barn swallow is the most widespread species of swallow in the world, occurring on all continents, with vagrants reported even in Antarctica.
The barn swallow is a bird of open country that normally nests in man-made structures and consequently has spread with human expansion.
The barn swallow is similar in its habits to other aerial insectivores, including other swallow species and the unrelated swifts.
The male barn swallow returns to the breeding grounds before the females and selects a nest site, which is then advertised to females with a circling flight and song.
Males sing to defend small territories and to attract mates.
The barn swallow is an attractive bird that feeds on flying insects and has therefore been tolerated by humans when it shares their buildings for nesting.

The same individuals often breed at the same site year after year, although settlement choices have been experimentally shown to be predicted by nest availability rather than any characteristics of available mates.
Hot dry summers will reduce the availability of insect food for chicks.
Its wingspan is about 32 cm.
It weighs about 18 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the barn swallow nests in people's buildings, and the tale answers: this bird of open country moved in with us.
It eats flying insects, so people let it stay, and as people spread, the swallow spread too.
The male comes back first and calls the females to his chosen nest site with a circling flight and song.
So it is that the same birds often return to the same place, year after year.

tagline.text: The guest who pays its rent in flying insects.

facts.text: The Caspian tern is the world's largest species of tern, with a subcosmopolitan but scattered distribution.
They feed mainly on fish, which they dive for, hovering high over the water and then plunging.
Breeding is in spring and summer, with one to three pale blue-green eggs, with heavy brown spotting, being laid.
The call is a loud heron-like croak.
They may fly up to 60 km from the breeding colony to catch fish; they often fish on freshwater lakes as well as at sea.
They nest either together in colonies, or singly in mixed colonies of other tern and gull species.
Their breeding habitat is large lakes and ocean coasts in North America, and locally in Europe, Asia, Africa, and Australasia.
North American birds migrate to southern coasts, the West Indies and northernmost South America.
Its wingspan is about 128 cm.
It weighs about 655 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the world's largest tern croaks loud like a heron.
The tale answers that it learned its voice in the long wait above the water, where it hovers high, then plunges like a stone for fish.
It ranges far for its catch, flying up to 60 km from the colony, over freshwater lakes and out at sea.
So it is that on large lakes and ocean coasts, that croak rings over colonies of terns and gulls.

tagline.text: The giant of terns, croaking like a heron, plunging for fish.

facts.text: Bullock's oriole is a small New World blackbird.
They mainly eat insects, berries, and nectar.
Mated pairs of Bullock's orioles cooperate to weave deep, pendant baskets in which are deposited between three and six eggs, though females tend to do much of the work.
In California, eucalyptus trees are used as major sources of nectar.
In some locations, they may be seen using hummingbird feeders.
The nest is woven of plant fibers, primarily bark and fine grass fiber, though animal hair is also commonly used.
They especially prefer riparian corridors, open deciduous woodland, and scrub forest.
In adult males, the tail is long, square, and jet black.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 29 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 38 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a hanging nest.
It lays 3 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The Bullock's oriole, a small New World blackbird, keeps to riverside trees and open woodland.
There the pair weaves a deep, hanging basket of bark, fine grass and animal hair.
Both mates work the threads, though the female does most of the weaving.
Into this hanging cradle the eggs are laid.
The tale answers that such fine work needs sweet fuel, so between meals of insects and berries it sips nectar from eucalyptus in California, and even from hummingbird feeders.

tagline.text: The little weaver who sips sweet nectar.

facts.text: The hooded oriole is a medium-sized New World oriole.
Their calls consist of whistling and wheets, while their song is a mixture of both.
The nest is a tightly woven pouch attached to the underside of a leaf or tree branch.
Sometimes their nest is filled with the egg of a brown-headed cowbird which is a parasite bird that lays its eggs in other birds nests for that species to take care of.
They forage in trees and shrubs, also feeding from flowers.
The male of this species ranges in color from a bright orange to a paler yellow, with a black back, face, tail and bib, with the wing containing two white bars.
The female is more of an olive color with some yellow accents.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 25 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 24 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in woodland.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The hooded oriole keeps to the trees and shrubs, hunting through the branches and feeding at flowers.
Beneath a leaf or branch it weaves a tight pouch, hanging its home from the underside of the green.
Its song mixes whistles and wheets, and they say it sings so the leaf will hold fast.
Yet sometimes a cowbird slips in an egg, and the oriole raises a stranger as its own.

tagline.text: A whistling weaver who hangs its home beneath the leaves.

facts.text: The dark-eyed junco is a species of junco, a group of small, grayish New World sparrows.
They mainly eat seeds and insects, with seeds comprising three quarters of their year-round diet.
Dark-eyed juncos usually nest in a cup-shaped depression on the ground, well-hidden by vegetation or other material, although nests are sometimes found in the lower branches of a shrub or tree.
In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders.
The song is a trill similar to the chipping sparrow's, except that the red-backed dark-eyed junco's song is more complex, similar to that of the yellow-eyed junco.
Young dark-eyed juncos also depend on a diet of mainly insects.
Normally, two clutches of four eggs are laid during the breeding season.
The call also resembles that of the black-throated blue warbler which is a member of the New World warbler family.
Its wingspan is about 25 cm.
It weighs about 20 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the dark-eyed junco keeps close to the earth, and the tale answers with its nest.
It hides a cup in a hollow on the ground, tucked out of sight under plants.
There it raises two clutches a season, feeding its young mostly on insects while it eats mostly seeds.
So it is that in winter this small gray sparrow comes into towns, the most common guest at many feeders.
Listen for its trill, like the chipping sparrow's.

tagline.text: Hidden ground nest, winter guest at the feeder.

facts.text: The loggerhead shrike is a passerine bird in the family Laniidae.
Due to its small size and weak talons, this predatory bird relies on impaling its prey upon thorns or barbed wire for facilitated consumption.
Although loggerhead shrikes are passerines, they are a predatory species that hunt during the day.
During this time, the male performs a courtship ritual that occurs in flight.
A distinctive alarm call is often given when threats from above are detected.
The bird requires an open habitat with an area to forage, elevated perches, and nesting sites.
The young then are released to the wild when they'd naturally disperse from their parents.
The beak is short, black, and hooked, and contains a tomial tooth to help tear into prey.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 29 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 52 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 9 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: Over open country, from high perches, the loggerhead shrike hunts by day, a small perching bird with a hunter's heart.
Ask why it hangs its catch on thorns and barbed wire.
Its talons are weak, the story says, so the thorn must hold what its feet cannot.
Then its short, black, hooked beak, with a tooth along its edge, tears the meal apart.
And when danger comes from above, it cries its own alarm.

tagline.text: The little hunter who sets its table on thorns.

facts.text: The California gull is a medium-sized gull, smaller on average than the herring gull, but larger on average than the ring-billed gull.
They mainly eat insects, fish and the eggs and young of other birds, especially ducklings.
The breeding habitat of the California gull are lakes and marshes in interior western North America from the Northwest Territories, Canada south to eastern California and Colorado.
Opportunistic feeders, California gulls often can be seen scavenging at garbage dumps, marinas and docks.
They nest in colonies, sometimes with other birds.
A monument in Salt Lake City commemorates this event, known as the "Miracle of the Gulls".
In California, the California gull at one time held the protected status California Species of Special Concern due to declining numbers at their historic California breeding colony at Mono Lake.
The California gull is the state bird of Utah, remembered for assisting Mormon settlers in dealing with a plague of Mormon crickets.
Its wingspan is about 121 cm.
It weighs about 683 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in coasts.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The California gull keeps to the inland lakes and marshes of western North America, nesting in colonies, sometimes beside other birds.
It turns down little: insects, fish, other birds' eggs and young, and scraps from dumps and docks.
So when a plague of crickets came upon the Mormon settlers, the gull is remembered as their helper.
Ask why it is Utah's state bird, and a Salt Lake City monument answers: the Miracle of the Gulls.

tagline.text: Utah's state bird, remembered for the Miracle of the Gulls.

facts.text: The ring-billed gull is a medium-sized gull native to North America, breeding in Canada and the northern Contiguous United States, and wintering mainly in the United States and northern Mexico.
Ring-billed gulls forage in flight or pick up objects while swimming, walking or wading.
They nest colonially on the ground, often on islands, but also increasingly on flat factory roofs.
In the late 19th century, the ring-billed gull was hunted for its plumage.
They are omnivorous; their diet may include insects, fish, grain, eggs, earthworms and rodents.
The specific delawarensis refers to the Delaware River.
The breeding habitat is near lakes, rivers, or the coast across most of Canada, and the northern United States.
The total population was estimated as 2.55 million birds in 2006, and still in 2018.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 120 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 516 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in coasts.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 3 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the ring-billed gull eats almost anything, and the tale answers that it never learned to choose.
Insects, fish, grain, eggs, earthworms, even rodents all go down.
It forages in flight, or picks things up while swimming, walking or wading.
At nesting time it crowds in with its kind on the ground, often on islands near lakes, rivers or the coast.
So it is that, more and more, its colonies now rise from flat factory roofs.

tagline.text: Fish or grain, island or rooftop: it makes do.

facts.text: Heermann's gull is a gull resident in the United States, Mexico and extreme southwestern British Columbia, nearly all nesting on Isla Rasa in the Gulf of California.
Heermann's gull eats small fish, marine invertebrates, lizards, insects, and carrion.
After the islands eroded away by 2007, the colony continued to nest on nearby rooftops.
Egg-collecting and disturbance during the breeding season are discouraged.
The nests are often at densities as high as 110 nests per 100 m2.
In June 2018, one of the colony's main nesting sites, the Seaside McDonald's, was destroyed by a drunk driving crash.
The success of the colony in any one year is dependent on the availability of prey and this is related to the ocean temperature changes brought about by El Niño.
They are usually found near shores or well out to sea, very rarely inland.
Its wingspan is about 114 cm.
It weighs about 500 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It lays 1 to 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: Ask where Heermann's gull keeps, and the tale points to shore and open sea.
Nearly all come home to one island, Isla Rasa in the Gulf of California, to nest packed close together.
They eat small fish, lizards, insects, sea creatures without backbones, and dead animals.
When one colony's islands wore away, the gulls did not leave; they nested on nearby rooftops.
So it is, they say, that this gull keeps its home even when the land is gone.

tagline.text: When the island wore away, it nested on the roofs.

And at each stop it calls a burry kabrick, the voice that sets it apart from look-alike kin.

tagline.text: The restless flycatcher with a burry, rough voice.

facts.text: The double-crested cormorant is a member of the cormorant family of water birds.
It mainly eats fish and hunts by swimming and diving.
They build stick nests in trees, on cliff edges, or on the ground on suitable islands.
Historically, the range extended west to the Near Islands, but possibly due to nest predation by introduced foxes, the birds were no longer breeding in the area by the mid-1930s.
After diving, it spends long periods standing with its wings outstretched to allow them to dry, since they are not fully waterproofed.
They are gregarious birds usually found in colonies, often with other aquatic birds, and have a deep, guttural grunt call.
Like all cormorants, the double-crested dives to find its prey.
It is found along the southern coast of Alaska and on the Aleutian Islands, ranging west from Kodiak to Chuginidak in the Aleutians.
Its wingspan is about 119 cm.
It weighs about 1.8 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the double-crested cormorant stands with its wings held open, and the tale begins underwater.
It hunts fish by swimming and diving, plunging down after its prey.
But its wings are not fully waterproofed, and they rise from each dive wet.
So it is that, after diving, it stands for long spells, wings outstretched like a cloak hung out to dry.
It waits in colonies that call with a deep, guttural grunt.

tagline.text: The diver who hangs its wings out to dry.

facts.text: The Hudsonian whimbrel or Hudsonian curlew is a wader in the large family Scolopacidae.
Before migration, berries become an important part of their diet.

In the mangroves of Colombia, whimbrel roost sites are located in close proximity to feeding territories and away from potential sources of mainland predators, but not away from areas of human disturbance.
The English name is imitative of the bird's call.
The nest is a bare scrape on tundra or Arctic moorland.
The usual call is a rippling whistle, prolonged into a trill for the song.
The Hudsonian whimbrel is a migratory coastal bird, wintering on coasts in southern North America and South America.
It is one of the most widespread of the curlews, breeding across much of subarctic North America.
Its wingspan is about 94 cm.
It weighs about 365 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in grassland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: Ask why the Hudsonian whimbrel is called by its own voice, and the tale begins on the tundra, where it keeps a bare scrape for a nest.
Its usual call is a rippling whistle, and when it sings, that whistle stretches into a long trill.
So it is that its English name was made to echo that call.
Before migration it feasts on berries, then winters on coasts as far as South America.

tagline.text: The bird that whistles its own name.

facts.text: The yellow-crowned night heron is one of two species of night heron in the genus Nyctanassa.
The young beg for food with a soft chu-chu-chu call that becomes louder as the chicks grow older and more demanding.
Their body size decreases from north to south, and the shape of their bills varies geographically, depending on the size of the crustaceans they eat in different regions.
Its habitat is closely linked to that of the crustaceans that make for most of its diet, and it tolerates fresh water, brackish water and saltwater.
The adults have virtually no predators, but the nests are vulnerable to other animals.
It can also feed on amphibians, molluscs, lizards, snakes, small rodents and small birds.
A different range of vocalizations plays an important part in courtship and pair formation.
In areas where the herons cohabit with people, they are often disturbed or shooed away from their nests if they get too close to human habitations.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 108 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 682 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where the yellow-crowned night heron keeps, and the answer is wherever the crustaceans are, in fresh water, brackish water or salt.
Crustaceans make up most of its meals, though it will also take amphibians, lizards, snakes and small rodents.
So it is that its bill changes shape from place to place, fitted to the size of the crustaceans it hunts there.
In the nest, its young beg with a soft chu-chu-chu that grows louder as they grow.

tagline.text: Wherever the crustaceans go, the night heron follows.

facts.text: In Australasia it is replaced by the closely related Nankeen night heron, with which it has hybridised in the area of contact.
Black-crowned night herons nest in colonies on platforms of sticks in a group of trees, or on the ground in protected locations such as islands or reedbeds.
A pair of adults were seen with two recently fledged juveniles in Somerset in 2017, which is the first proven breeding record of wild black-crowned night herons in Great Britain.
One to eight long slender white plumes, erected in greeting and courtship displays, extend from the back of the head.
Three to eight eggs are laid.
Their resting posture is normally somewhat hunched but when hunting they extend their necks and look more like other wading birds.
During the day they rest in dense trees or bushes.
The epithet nycticorax is from Ancient Greek and combines nux, nuktos meaning "night" and korax meaning "raven".
Its wingspan is about 105 cm.
It weighs about 810 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 1 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Its old Greek name means night raven, yet by day it keeps to dense trees and bushes, hunched.
Ask why it folds itself so small, and the tale answers that it is hiding its reach for the hunt.
For when it hunts fish in the wetlands, it stretches out its neck and looks like any other wader.
When it greets or courts, it raises long white plumes from the back of its head.

tagline.text: The night raven folds small by day and stretches tall to hunt.

facts.text: The ruddy duck is a species of duck, one of six extant species of stiff-tailed duck.
Ruddy ducks mainly feed on a large amount of plant matter like seeds and roots as well as aquatic insects and crustaceans.
Unlike other migratory anatine courtship where partnerships occur in wintering grounds, ruddy ducks often begin courtship on the breeding ground.
Males are known to produce short "aa-anh" calls and other noises in short bursts.
It has a short and stout scoop-shaped bill designed for underwater foraging.
The food foraged is done underwater, an activity that the ruddy duck excels at.
In courting, a bubbling male orientates his body laterally to the female.
Female ruddy ducks have a much higher pitched call, often having a "raanh" sound when communicating with their brood, squeaks when chased by males, and hisses and nasal sounds towards intruders.
Its wingspan is about 58 cm.
It weighs about 608 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 5 to 15 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the ruddy duck dives, and the tale begins with its bill: short and stout, shaped like a scoop for the work below.
Underwater it forages best of all, gathering seeds and roots, water insects and crustaceans.
It courts not in a wintering place but on the breeding ground itself.
There the bubbling male turns his body sideways to the female, calling his short "aa-anh" in bursts.
So it is: a scoop below, a bubbler courting above.

tagline.text: Scoop-billed diver, bubbling suitor of the wetlands.

facts.text: The osprey, historically known as sea hawk, river hawk, and fish hawk, is a diurnal, fish-eating bird of prey with a cosmopolitan range.
The osprey is piscivorous, with fish making up 99% of its diet.
The nest is a large heap of sticks, driftwood, turf, or seaweed built in forks of trees, rocky outcrops, utility poles, artificial platforms, or offshore islets.
Evidence indicates regional decline in South Australia, where former territories at locations in the Spencer Gulf and along the lower Murray River have been vacant for decades.
The osprey differs in several respects from other diurnal birds of prey.
It lives in a wide variety of habitats and nests in locations near a body of water providing an adequate food supply.
The species rarely scavenges dead or dying fish.
If no nesting sites are available, young ospreys may be forced to delay breeding.
Its wingspan is about 164 cm.
It weighs about 1.5 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 1 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the osprey was once called sea hawk, river hawk and fish hawk, and the tale answers: fish is nearly all it ever eats.
It hunts by day, the world over, and seldom stoops to dead fish.
So it keeps near water that can feed it, heaping its great nest of sticks, driftwood, turf and seaweed in tree forks and on rocks.
Where no nest place is left, the young must wait to raise their own.

tagline.text: Sea hawk, river hawk, fish hawk: by any name, a fisher.

facts.text: The house sparrow is a bird of the sparrow family Passeridae, found in most parts of the world.
Females and young birds are coloured pale brown and grey, and males have brighter black, white, and brown markings.
It roosts communally while breeding nests are usually grouped together in clumps.
Birds breeding for the first time are rarely successful in raising young, and reproductive success increases with age, as older birds breed earlier in the breeding season, and fledge more young.
Transcribed as chirrup, tschilp, or philip, this note is made as a contact call by flocking or resting birds; or by males to proclaim nest ownership and invite pairing.
From around 1560 to at least the 19th century in northern Europe, earthenware "sparrow pots" were hung from eaves to attract nesting birds so the young could be readily harvested.
It reaches its greatest densities in urban centres, but its reproductive success is greater in suburbs, where insects are more abundant.
After fledging and leaving the care of their parents, young sparrows have a high mortality rate, which lessens as they grow older and more experienced.
Its wingspan is about 24 cm.
It weighs about 26 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a cavity, a ball-shaped nest or a crevice.
It lays 1 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The house sparrow keeps to towns and farms all year, crowding its nests together in clumps and roosting together with its flock.
Ask why the sparrow chatters so, and the tale answers: in such a crowd, each bird calls 'chirrup' or 'philip' to say, I am here.
Males use that same note to claim a nest and invite a mate.
So it is that old sparrows do best: they nest earlier and fledge more young than first-timers.

tagline.text: Chirrup! The crowd-loving voice of farm and town.

facts.text: The Savannah sparrow is a small New World sparrow that is the only member of the genus Passerculus.
They mainly eat seeds, but also eat insects in the breeding season.
They are typically encountered as pairs or family groups in the breeding season, and assemble in flocks for the winter migration.
It is a widespread and abundant species that occupies open grassland habitats in North America.
Wilson had first seen the species on the coast near Savannah, Georgia.
Over most of its range it is migratory, breeding in Canada and the northern United States while wintering in Mexico and the southern United States.
The Pacific and Mexican breeders are resident, but other populations are migratory, wintering from the southern United States across Central America and the Caribbean to northern South America.
The Savannah sparrow has a typically sparrow-like dark-streaked brown back, and whitish underparts with brown or blackish breast and flank streaking.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 22 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 20 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in grassland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: A small brown sparrow keeps the open grasslands of North America, its back streaked dark, its pale breast lined with brown.
In the breeding season it keeps in pairs and families, eating insects as well as seeds.
Then, so the story goes, the families remember the crowd and gather in flocks to fly south for winter.
So it is that this bird of the grass bears a coastal name, for Wilson first met it near Savannah, Georgia.

tagline.text: A grassland sparrow named for the coast where it was found.

facts.text: The lazuli bunting is a North American songbird named for the gemstone lapis lazuli.
They eat mostly seeds and insects.
It makes a loose cup nest of grasses and rootlets placed in a bush.
The song is a high, rapid, strident warble, similar to that of the indigo bunting but longer and with less repetition.
They may feed conspicuously on the ground or in bushes, but singing males are often very elusive in treetops.
It lays three or four pale blue eggs.
On the Pacific coast their breeding range extends south to extreme northwestern Baja California.
