The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the lazuli bunting, named for a gemstone, hides when it sings.
It feeds in plain sight, on the ground or in bushes, taking seeds and insects.
But a singing male slips into the treetops, pouring out his high, rapid warble where few eyes find him.
They say he draws eyes upward, away from a loose grass cup in a bush and its pale blue eggs.

tagline.text: A gem-named singer, heard high and hard to find.

facts.text: The band-tailed pigeon is a pigeon native to the Americas, and one of the largest pigeons in this region.
Its voice is low-pitched and owl-like, often in two-syllable calls that rise and then fall with even spacing between calls.
Band-tailed pigeons form pairs to build nests, with the female building the nests in trees out of twigs, often closely together to form small colonies.
Band-tailed pigeons are nomadic feeders, changing their diet along the seasons, and will travel up to 5 km away from their nests to feed.
While forest management can help these birds in terms of nesting habitats, they rely heavily on hardwoods and fruit and nut producing shrubs for food during breeding seasons.
It builds a rudimentary platform nest out of twigs, in which it lays one or two eggs.
Usually, there is just one egg in a clutch, occasionally two; about 8% of nests have two eggs.
As forest birds, they feed from the floor and from trees.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 62 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 366 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a platform.
It lays 1 to 3 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the band-tailed pigeon, among the largest pigeons of the Americas, calls low like an owl.
Its song rises and then falls, call after call, with even pauses between.
The tale answers that it calls to keep near its neighbors, whose twig nests sit close in small tree colonies.
Yet it wanders far from its nest to feed, changing its food with the seasons.
So each rough platform most often holds just one egg.

tagline.text: Low owl-voice of the forest, wanderer of the seasons.

facts.text: The Indian peafowl, also known as the common peafowl, or blue peafowl, is a species of peafowl native to the Indian subcontinent.
The peafowl lives mainly on the ground in open forests or on cultivable lands where it forages for berries and grains, and also preys on snakes, lizards and small rodents.
The Indian peafowl forages on the ground in small groups, known as musters, that usually have a single peacock and three to five peahens.
They maintain small territories next to each other and allow females to visit them, but make no attempt to guard harems, and females do not favour specific males.
A golden peacock is considered as a symbol of Ashkenazi Jewish culture, and is the subject of several folktales and songs in Yiddish.
Poaching of peacocks for their meat and feathers and accidental poisoning by feeding on pesticide treated seeds are known threats to wild birds.
Young males also resemble the females with chestnut colored primaries.
It makes loud calls, which makes it easier to detect, and are often used to indicate the presence of a predator in the forest areas.
It weighs about 4.2 kg.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It nests in a scrape on the ground.
It lays 3 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the peafowl keeps to the ground, and the tale points to the open forests and farm fields of the Indian subcontinent.
There it forages in small groups called musters, a peacock walking among several peahens, picking up berries and grains.
It hunts snakes, lizards and small rodents as well.
And when a predator slips between the trees, its loud calls ring out to tell of the danger.
So the tale names it the watchman of the forest.

tagline.text: The loud watchman of the forest floor.

facts.text: The American white pelican is a large aquatic soaring bird from the order Pelecaniformes.
American white pelicans nest in colonies of several hundred pairs on islands in remote brackish and freshwater lakes of inland North America.
The birds arrive on the breeding grounds in March or April; nesting starts between early April and early June.
It has the California Department of Fish and Game protective status California species of special concern.
The horn is shed after the birds mate and lay their eggs.
The most northerly nesting colony can be found on islands in the rapids of the Slave River between Fort Fitzgerald, Alberta and Fort Smith, Northwest Territories.
The nest is a shallow depression scraped in the ground, into which some twigs, sticks, reeds, or similar debris have been gathered.
Habitat loss is the largest known cause of nesting failure, with flooding and drought being recurrent problems.
Its wingspan is about 247 cm.
It weighs about 5.6 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.

It spends most of its time on or in water.

sentences.text: Ask why the American white pelican, a great soaring bird, seeks lonely islands in far inland lakes.
The tale answers that it wants trusted company: there it nests among several hundred pairs, each scraping a shallow dip and gathering in twigs, sticks and reeds.
They say it wears its horn only for courting, and once the mating is done and the eggs are laid, it lets the horn fall away.
So it is: no horn, eggs to keep.

tagline.text: It keeps its horn only until the eggs are laid.

facts.text: The brown pelican is a bird of the pelican family, Pelecanidae, one of three species found in the Americas and one of two that feed by diving into water.
The brown pelican is a very gregarious bird; it lives in flocks of both sexes throughout the year.
Nesting season peaks during March and April.
The brown pelican is now a staple of crowded coastal regions and is at some risk by fishermen and boaters.
After nesting, North American birds move in flocks further north along the coasts, returning to warmer waters for winter.
In 1903, Theodore Roosevelt set aside Pelican Island, now known as Pelican Island National Wildlife Refuge, to solely protect the brown pelican from hunters.
The lower mandible is blackish, with a greenish-black gular pouch at the bottom for draining water when it scoops out prey.
The brown pelican mainly feeds on fish, but occasionally eats amphibians, crustaceans, and the eggs and nestlings of birds.

It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time in the air.
It nests in a mound or a platform.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the brown pelican drops from the sky, and the tale answers: it is diving for fish.
Among the pelicans of the Americas, it is one of the divers.
It scoops its catch into a greenish-black pouch, and the pouch drains the water away.
Mostly it eats fish, and now and then the eggs and chicks of other birds.
So it is never alone, for it lives in flocks of males and females all year round.

tagline.text: It drops from the sky and drains the sea from its pouch.

facts.text: The cliff swallow or American cliff swallow is a member of the passerine bird family Hirundinidae, the swallows and martins.
Cliff swallows are extremely social songbirds that can be found in large nesting colonies reaching over 2,000 nests.
Cliff swallows live in a colonial lifestyle during the breeding season, composed of a large number of pairs per nesting site.
They usually arrive in large groups and start immediately to choose their nesting sites.
Juvenile cliff swallows are said to have established a unique call by the approximate age of 15 days, which allows the parents to identify their chick from others in the colony.
As their name suggests, throughout history the cliff swallows concentrated their nesting colonies along mountain cliffs, primarily by the western North American coast.
The pre-formative facial plumage has been suggested as a possible way for parents nesting in large colonies to recognize their chicks.
They are frequently seen flying overhead in large flocks during migration, gracefully foraging over fields for flying insects or perching tightly together on a wire preening under the sun.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 33 cm from its wing length.

It lives mostly in grassland.

It spends most of its time in the air.

The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Along the mountain cliffs of western North America's coast, cliff swallows pack their ball-shaped nests into colonies that can top 2,000.
Ask how a parent finds its own chick among so many, and the tale answers: each young one soon has a call all its own.
Its parents know that voice from all the rest, and some say they know its face too.
So it is, the story goes, that no chick is a stranger on the crowded cliff.

tagline.text: In a city of nests, every chick has its own call.

facts.text: The phainopepla or northern phainopepla is the most northerly representative of the mainly tropical Central American family Ptiliogonatidae, the silky flycatchers.
Their diet consists of berries, any small insects, fruits, vegetables.

sentences.text: Near water, in thickets and open woods, the phainopepla lays a loose nest of twigs and mosses on a tree branch.
Its name means "shining robe," for the male's plumage, and the tale says a bird so finely dressed wanted fine voices to match.
So it is that the phainopepla copies the calls of twelve other birds, even the red-tailed hawk.
Between borrowed calls, it fills its short, slender bill with berries and small insects.

tagline.text: The shining robe that sings in borrowed voices.

facts.text: The common poorwill is a nocturnal bird of the family Caprimulgidae, the nightjars.
Like other members of this family it feeds on nocturnal insects such as moths, beetles, and grasshoppers.
The nest of the common poorwill is a shallow scrape on the ground, often at the base of a hill and frequently shaded partly by a bush or clump of grass.
The outer tail-feathers are tipped with white, the markings slightly more prominent in the male.
The common poorwill frequently takes prey off of the ground or by leaping into the air from the ground.
The clutch size is typically two, and the eggs are white to creamy, or pale pink, sometimes with darker mottling.
Like many other nightjars, the common name derives from its call, a monotonous poor-will given from dusk to dawn.

sentences.text: Ask why the poorwill sings its own name, and the tale begins in the dry, open country of grass, shrub and stony desert slope.
There, from dusk to dawn, it calls poor-will, poor-will, the same plain call again and again.
It hunts the night from the ground, leaping up into the dark to snatch moths, beetles and grasshoppers.
So the story goes, it calls its name all night so the dark will not forget it.

tagline.text: The night bird that leaps from the ground and calls its name.

facts.text: The black-headed grosbeak is a medium-sized, seed-eating bird in the family Cardinalidae.

It is sometimes considered conspecific with the rose-breasted grosbeak with which it hybridizes on the American Great Plains.

sentences.text: In forests from the Pacific Coast to the mountains of Mexico, the black-headed grosbeak builds an open saucer of grass, twigs, bark and conifer needles.
It is named a seed-eater, and it does eat pine seeds, berries and fruit.
Yet in summer it turns hunter of spiders, snails and insects.
Ask why it flies south early in the fall and returns late in spring.
The tale answers: it waits until the north is crawling with its summer feast.

tagline.text: Seed-eater by name, spider hunter by summer.

facts.text: The spotted towhee is a large New World sparrow.
The call may be harsher and more varied than for the eastern towhee.
During the breeding season they mainly eat insects, ground dwelling beetles, spiders and other arthropods that reside in the leaf litter that is foraged by the spotted towhee.

They only eat protein rich food in the breeding season, and in the fall and winter they focus on foraging for acorns, seeds, oats, and berries.
The female builds the nest over a period of about five days.
The spotted towhee lives in dry upland forests, open forests, brushy fields, and chaparrals.

There, beneath dense and continuous cover, it seeks its food, mostly on the ground, about two-thirds of the time.

So the story goes that a bird so hidden must be heard instead: a striking and exuberant songster, famed for mimicking others.

tagline.text: The hidden singer of the chaparral floor.

facts.text: The greater yellowlegs is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They mainly eat insects and small fish, as well as crustaceans, marine worms, frogs, seeds and berries.
They nest on the ground, usually in well-hidden locations near water.
The call is harsher, louder, and clearer than that of the lesser yellowlegs.
The young leave the nest within 24 hours of hatching and then leave the vicinity of the nest within two days.
Their breeding habitat is bogs and marshes in the boreal forest region of Canada and Alaska.
They migrate to the Atlantic and Pacific coasts of the United States, the Caribbean, and south to South America.
The greater yellowlegs is similar in appearance to the smaller lesser yellowlegs.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 64 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 162 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in wetlands.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Near Threatened.

sentences.text: In the bogs and marshes of the northern forests of Canada and Alaska, the greater yellowlegs hides its nest on the ground near water.
Ask why its young are gone so soon, and the tale says they hatch restless.
Within a day the chicks leave the nest, and soon they leave the place where it stood.
So, the story goes, it calls louder and harsher than its look-alike cousin, the lesser yellowlegs, so its wandering chicks can hear.

tagline.text: The loud shorebird whose chicks never stay home.

facts.text: The willet is a large shorebird in the family Scolopacidae.
They are territorial both on the breeding grounds and on the wintering areas but form loose breeding colonies or wintering groups.
The male normally leads the female through the territory and creates trial nest scrapes for the female to consider until she selects the site.
The willet's name is onomatopoeic and refers to its loud piercing "pill-will-willet" territorial song., which is higher pitched and repeated at a faster rate in Eastern willets than in Western birds.
The passage of the Migratory Bird Treaty Act in 1918 protected the willet from intensive exploitation by hunters for food and allowed its numbers to rebound to present levels.
When displaying the wings are held stiffly and downcurved in flight while on the ground the display gives prominence to the distinctive pattern of the underwings.
If the nest is placed among grass the female may pull grass stalks over the nest for camouflage.
The eastern willet breeds in coastal saltmarshes while the western willet breeds in freshwater prairie marshes, sloughs, potholes and other inland wetlands.
Its wingspan is about 70 cm.
It weighs about 246 g.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in coasts.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the willet shouts its own name across the marsh, and the tale answers: so every neighbor knows whose ground this is.
Its loud, piercing "pill-will-willet" rings over eastern saltmarsh and inland prairie marsh alike.
At nesting time, the male leads the female through his ground, scraping trial nests until she chooses.
If the spot is in grass, she may pull the stalks over it to hide it.
So it is: a loud bird, a hidden nest.

tagline.text: It shouts its own name, then hides its nest in grass.

facts.text: The house wren complex has been split into eight species: Northern house wren, Troglodytes aedon Southern house wren, Troglodytes musculus Cozumel wren, Troglodytes beani Kalinago wren, Troglodytes martinicensis St.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 16 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 11 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It lays its eggs in other birds' nests.
It lays 4 to 8 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the northern house wren never leaves its shrubland; the tale answers that the tangle is home enough.
All year it stays, perched in trees and shrubs, never far from its thicket.
There it feeds on insects and other little creatures without backbones.
Once it was counted as one house wren with its cousins, but that group is now split into eight kinds.
So the little wren keeps its thicket, rated Least Concern.

tagline.text: Home all year in the shrubland tangle.

facts.text: The American robin is a migratory bird of the true thrush genus and Turdidae, the wider thrush family.
The species is active mostly during the day and assembles in large flocks at night.
The species is one of the first North American birds to lay eggs, and normally has two to three broods per breeding season, which lasts from April to July.
The male, as with many thrushes, has a complex and almost continuous song.
The Tlingit people of northwestern North America held it to be a culture hero created by Raven to please the people with its song.
Juveniles and eggs are preyed upon by squirrels, snakes, and some birds.
Its diet consists of invertebrates, fruits, and berries.
The flocks break up during the day when the birds feed on fruits and berries in smaller groups.
Its wingspan is about 39 cm.
It weighs about 78 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the male robin sings almost without stopping, and the Tlingit of northwestern North America once answered: Raven made it to please the people with its song.
By day the robins scatter in small groups to feed on fruits and berries, and on insects and other creatures without backbones.
When night falls, they gather again in great flocks, as if to guard that song till morning, so the tale goes.

tagline.text: Made by Raven to please the people with song.

facts.text: The western kingbird is a large tyrant flycatcher found throughout western North America, as far south as Mexico.
Kingbirds make a sturdy cup nest in a tree or shrub, sometimes on top of a pole or other man-made structure.
Vocalizations from this species often consist of a long series of squeaky bubbling calls, sometimes compared to a squeaky toy.
Adults are a combination of both gray and yellow plumage, along with crimson feathers that are hidden until courtship or against intruders.
Three to five white, creamy, or pinkish eggs with heavy blotches of brown, black, or lavender are laid and incubated for 12 to 14 days.
Characteristic of kingbird species, the western kingbird is very territorial.
The breeding habitat is open areas in western North America.
Instances of hybridization with the closely related Eastern Kingbird have been reported.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 37 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 40 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Across the open west of North America, the western kingbird perches in tree and shrub.
There it builds a sturdy cup nest, sometimes atop a pole.
Like all kingbirds, it guards its ground fiercely.
Ask why it wears plain gray and yellow, and the tale answers: it hides its crimson feathers, saving them for courtship or for intruders.
Its voice is no royal trumpet, only a long run of squeaky, bubbling calls, like a squeaky toy.

tagline.text: Hidden crimson, saved for courtship and for intruders.

facts.text: Cassin's kingbird is a large tyrant flycatcher native to western North America.
They build a bulky nest on a horizontal tree limb in mid-story or the canopy of trees.
The three to five spotted white eggs have an incubation period of 18 to 19 days.
The type locality is Temascaltepec, Mexico.
In the summer, these birds can be found in California and from Montana to Utah, along the eastern Rocky Mountains.
Adults have a gray head with slightly darker cheeks; a dark unforked tail with a buffy fringe and gray-olive underparts.
The name of this bird commemorates the American ornithologist John Cassin.
Their habitat includes rangelands and savannas.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 38 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 46 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 2 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Out on the western rangelands and savannas keeps Cassin's kingbird, a large tyrant flycatcher with a gray head and a dark, unforked tail.
It spends its days perched in trees, living on insects and other small creatures.
Ask why its nest is so bulky, and the tale answers: it rests on a level limb high in the canopy, and a wide branch asks for a wide home.
There its spotted white eggs lie, up among the leaves.

tagline.text: The gray-headed tyrant perched above the western rangelands.

facts.text: The barn owl is recognized by most taxonomic authorities.
Like most owls, it is nocturnal, relying on its acute sense of hearing when hunting in complete darkness.
Barn owls living in tropical regions can breed at any time of year, but some seasonality in nesting is still evident.
Intensification of agricultural practices often means that the rough grassland that provides the best foraging habitat is lost.
Nestlings are covered in white down, but the heart-shaped facial disk becomes visible soon after hatching.
It often becomes active shortly before dusk and can sometimes be seen during the day when relocating from one roosting site to another.
Where there are distinct wet and dry seasons, egg-laying usually takes place during the dry season, with increased rodent prey becoming available to the birds as the vegetation dies off.
An insufficiency of suitable nesting sites may be another factor limiting barn owl numbers.
Its wingspan is about 98 cm.
It weighs about 403 g.
It feeds mostly on other vertebrates.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cavity or a crevice.
It lays 1 to 7 eggs in a clutch.

sentences.text: When dusk is near, the barn owl wakes, and through the black night it hunts by ear alone.
Where the year splits into wet and dry, it lays its eggs when the dry days come.
For then the grass dies back, they say, and more rodents come within its reach.
So it is that its downy white chicks, heart-faced, wake to plenty.
It keeps to farms and towns all year, wherever a hollow waits to hold its nest.

tagline.text: Hunter by ear, waking when the daylight fades.

facts.text: Brandt's cormorant is a strictly marine bird of the cormorant family of seabirds that inhabits the Pacific coast of North America.
They breed between March and August, and usually have four eggs.
Young birds are cared for by both parents.
Brandt's cormorants live on the Pacific coast of North America, in habitats such as bays, estuaries, and lagoons.
It ranges, in the summer, from Alaska to the Gulf of California, but the population north of Vancouver Island migrates south during the winter.
The IOU followed this classification in 2021.
Año Nuevo Island is an important seabird breeding colony in the Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary, hosting Brandt's cormorants among other species of seabirds.
During the breeding season, adults have a blue throat patch.
Its wingspan is about 108 cm.
It weighs about 2.2 kg.
It feeds mostly on fish and other animals it catches in water.
It lives mostly in the open sea.
Some of its populations migrate and others stay all year.
It spends most of its time on or in water.
It lays 1 to 6 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Along the Pacific coast of North America, Brandt's cormorant keeps to the sea, to its bays, estuaries and lagoons, catching fish in the water.
Ask why its throat turns blue, and the tale answers: from March to August, when it breeds, the sea lends it a patch of its own color.
Both parents tend the young, and Año Nuevo Island is one of the colonies where they breed.
In winter, the birds north of Vancouver Island travel south.

tagline.text: The sea lends it blue each breeding season.

facts.text: The pin-tailed whydah is a small songbird with a conspicuous pennant-like tail in breeding males.
The species is a brood parasite which lays its eggs in the nests of estrildid finches, especially waxbills.
Unlike the common cuckoo, it does not destroy the host's eggs.
It is a resident breeding bird in most of Africa south of the Sahara Desert.
The pin-tailed whydah occurs in much of sub-Saharan Africa, favouring grassland, scrubs and savannah, also coming into parks and gardens.
In Portugal it is established in the region around Aveiro, with observations occurring north and south of it.
The adult male has a black back and crown, and a very long black tail.
The wings are dark brown with white patches, and the underparts and the head, apart from the crown, are white.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 21 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 16 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays its eggs without building a nest.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: On the grassland, scrub and savannah south of the Sahara lives a small songbird that stays there all year.
The male wears a black crown and a very long black tail, like a pennant.
It builds no nest of its own, but lays its eggs in the nests of waxbills.
Yet unlike the cuckoo, it breaks none of the host's eggs.
So the story goes, that is the bargain: the finch lends a nest, and the whydah spares its eggs.

tagline.text: A borrowed nest, and every host egg left whole.

facts.text: Bell's vireo is a songbird that migrates between a breeding range in Western North America and a winter range in Central America.
Bell's vireos construct a hanging nest suspended between the ends of low tree branches.
In its breeding range, Bell's vireo often uses dense shrubbery in riparian areas or otherwise near water.
It is dull olive-gray above and whitish below.
It has a faint white eye ring and faint wing bars.
Consideration of Bell's vireo has been a factor in several land development projects, to protect least Bell's vireo habitat.
The decline of the least Bell's vireo is mostly due to a loss of riparian habitat.
The least Bell's vireo is an endangered subspecies in Southern California.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 17 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 8.5 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a hanging nest.
It lays 3 to 4 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where Bell's vireo raises its young: in dense shrubs near water across western North America.
Dull olive-gray above, it hunts insects among the branches.
It hangs its nest between the ends of low branches, a cradle slung in the air.
So the story goes, bird and riverside thicket are bound together; lose the thicket, and the bird fades.
In Southern California the least Bell's vireo is endangered, and builders must now plan around it.

tagline.text: A cradle hung between branch tips, beside the water.

facts.text: The warbling vireo is a small North American songbird.
It often nests in widely spaced trees, often cottonwood or aspen, along streams or rivers.
Warbling vireos forage for insects in trees, hopping along branches and sometimes hovering.
They make a deep cup nest suspended from a tree branch or shrub, placed relatively high in the east and lower in the west.
The male helps with incubation and may sing from the nest.
The song is a cheerful warble, similar to that of the painted bunting and the purple finch.
Its breeding habitat is open deciduous and mixed woods from Alaska to Mexico.
It migrates to Mexico and Central America.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 22 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 13 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask why the warbling vireo hangs its cup nest from a branch, in the cottonwoods and aspens along the rivers.
The tale answers that it is a cup made for holding song.
For the male takes his turn warming the eggs, and as he sits, he may sing his cheerful warble from the nest.
This small songbird hops along branches and sometimes hovers, hunting insects.
So the woods from Alaska to Mexico ring with its warble.

tagline.text: The bird that sings from its own nest.

facts.text: Hutton's vireo is a small songbird in the family Vireonidae, the vireos, greenlets, and shrike-babblers.
Hutton's vireo feeds primarily on insects but also includes spiders and small fruits in its diet.
The most common clutch size is four eggs but clutches of one to five have been found.
The song of Hutton's vireo is highly variable among individuals and populations.
It forages methodically, taking prey mostly by gleaning from leaves but also from flowers, twigs, and bark, sometimes hanging upside-down to do so.
The eggs are white with a few dark spots.
The species sings throughout the day and throughout the year, typically from a somewhat hidden perch in the forest subcanopy or canopy.
In Guatemala V. h. vulcani inhabits pine-oak forest and pine savanna.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 20 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 11 g.
It feeds mostly on insects and other invertebrates.
It lives mostly in forest.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time perched in trees and shrubs.
It nests in a ball-shaped nest.
It lays 1 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where Hutton's vireo keeps, and the tale points up, to a somewhat hidden perch high in the forest.
From there this small songbird sings all day and all year, and each one sings its own way.
It hunts slowly and carefully, picking insects and spiders from leaves, flowers, twigs and bark, sometimes hanging upside-down.
So the story goes: a bird that sings all year must hunt all year, and never rushes a single leaf.

tagline.text: A hidden voice in the treetops, singing all day, all year.

facts.text: The mourning dove is a member of the dove family, Columbidae.
Mourning doves eat almost exclusively seeds, but the young are fed crop milk by their parents.
Outside the breeding season, mourning doves roost communally in dense deciduous trees or conifers.
Courtship begins with a noisy flight by the male, followed by a graceful, circular glide with outstretched wings and head down.
During the call, the throat of the dove swells.
The "mourning" part of its common name comes from its doleful call.
Migration is usually during the day, in flocks, and at low altitudes.
As a gamebird, the mourning dove is well-managed, with more than 20 million shot by hunters each year.
Its wingspan is about 43 cm.
It weighs about 119 g.
It feeds mostly on seeds.
It lives mostly in towns, farms and other places people have changed.
It stays in its range all year.
It spends most of its time on the ground.
It lays 2 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: The mourning dove keeps mostly to the ground, picking up seeds on farms and in towns.
When it calls, its throat swells, and out comes the doleful song that gave the bird its name.
Ask why it sounds so sad, and the tale answers: though it eats almost nothing but seeds, it must feed its young on crop milk.
So, they say, its sorrow is only the sound of a busy parent.

tagline.text: Its sad song is only a busy parent's sigh.

facts.text: The golden-crowned sparrow is a large New World sparrow found in the western part of North America.
The golden-crowned sparrow spends its winters in flocks with conspecifics, but also often with other sparrow species, especially white-crowned sparrows.
Males on the breeding ground sing throughout the day from an exposed perch.
The song is a three-note whistle, descending in pitch.
As with other flock-living passerines, the golden-crowned sparrow is prone to elevated levels of feather mites.
Flock territories typically range in size from 15–20 acres.
The nest is a bulky cup built by the female.
The call also sounds like the words I'm so weary, so Alaskan gold miners along the trails called this bird "Weary Willie".
Its wingspan is estimated at about 24 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 32 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 5 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Out in the western shrublands of North America, the golden-crowned sparrow spends its winters in flocks, often mixed with white-crowned sparrows.
On the breeding grounds, the males sing all day from an open perch, a whistle of three notes falling in pitch.
Ask why its call sounds so tired, and the tale answers that it is saying "I'm so weary."
So it is that Alaskan gold miners along the trails named this bird Weary Willie.

tagline.text: The whistler the gold miners called Weary Willie.

facts.text: The white-crowned sparrow is a species of passerine bird native to North America.
They mainly eat seeds, other plant parts and insects.
In winter, they often forage in flocks.
It breeds in brushy areas in the taiga and tundra of the northernmost parts of the continent and in the Rocky Mountains and Pacific coast.
The scientific name is from Ancient Greek.
Their breeding habitat is brushy areas across northern Canada and the western United States.
Adults have black and white stripes on their head, a gray face, brown streaked upper parts and a long tail.
A medium-sized member of the New World sparrow family, this species is marked by a grey face and black and white streaking on the upper head.
Its wingspan is estimated at about 24 cm from its wing length.
It weighs about 28 g.
It eats a wide mix of foods.
It lives mostly in shrubland.
It migrates between breeding and wintering grounds.
It forages in the air, on the ground and in the trees alike.
It nests in a cup.
It lays 3 to 7 eggs in a clutch.
The IUCN Red List rates it Least Concern.

sentences.text: Ask where the white-crowned sparrow keeps, and the answer is brush, in the far north's taiga and tundra and along the Rocky Mountains and Pacific coast.
It builds a cup nest and eats seeds, plant parts and insects.
In winter it forages in flocks.
Why the black and white stripes above its gray face?
The tale answers that they are snow and shadow from the north, worn as a crown wherever it goes.

tagline.text: A crown of snow and shadow, carried from the north.
